Seminar Title:

A Study on Geomechanical Characterization of Faults and its Influence on Slope Stability Using Physical and Numerical Modelling

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Mining Engineering

Speaker Name:

Mohammed Asif ( Rollno : 521mn1003)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar hall, MN Department

Date and Time:

20 May 2026 5.00 PM

Contact:

Ram Manohar Bishwal

Abstract:

Characterization of major geological discontinuities, such as faults, during feasibility studies and in the early stage of mine opening remains challenging due to their inaccessibility, difficulties in collecting representative fault gouge, and the presence of high spatial variability along the fault length and/or dip. These limitations often pose serious geotechnical and safety risks and have been a precursor to several instabilities in both opencast and underground mines. The risk from faults is influenced not only by their own characteristics but also by the interplay between fault geometry, material properties, and operational processes (e.g., excavation size &amp orientation and stress redistribution). Due to the alteration of the mining-induced stress regime, it may trigger fault reactivation, leading to hazards and instabilities such as water inrush, rock bursts, gas leakage, and other operational risks. Furthermore, the aspects of fault reactivation and fault-slip-based slope failure mechanisms are not adequately studied, especially in Indian opencast coal mines. The study proposes an investigation into the structural, microstructural, and geo-mechanical characteristics of fault zones, their influence on slope stability and fault reactivation, and the potential for fault-induced slope failure through integrated numerical and physical modelling.

For a preliminary understanding of the nature of fault distribution in Indian coalfields vis-&agrave-vis exploration adequacy, the study started with the collection of data from over &gt 200 mines (under different stages of exploration). It was found that slope instability was influenced by fault density, and there is a correlation between fault density and exploration level (R2 = 0.53). Surprisingly, over 53% of the coal blocks lack any fault-related data in their borehole information, casting doubt on exploration practices. Among those case studies, mines with &gt 3.5 faults/km2 were observed to be affected by major operational geotechnical challenges.

To enhance the quantification of structural complexity, the study further integrates fractal dimension and the fault-influence factor, which were subsequently applied to eight large opencast mines. Based on these parameters, the mines were subsequently classified into moderate and relatively complex categories, with good validation of the observed geotechnical and operational instability conditions. A logistic regression model incorporating the Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) was also developed to predict the failure of slope induced by faults. The model determined that the threshold values for FIF &ge 0.44 and Db &ge 1.42 yield a failure probability greater than 65%.

As the collection of fault gouge/infill materials and the associated damaged zone is often very challenging due to minimal exposure and accessibility at fault outcrops, only limited fault gouge samples (from four coal mines) could be collected. Therefore, the practice of using remoulded samples or synthetic equivalent materials as fault gouges was planned. To ascertain the nature of the fault gouge composition and identify a suitable equivalent material, mineralogical and microstructural investigations based on XRD and SEM analysis were conducted. The laboratory analysis showed a prevalence of clay minerals (kaolinite (27.7%) and illite (29%)). Further, to identify the equivalent material, kaolinite was chosen and confirmed as suitable based on both microstructural analysis and the literature. To assess the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) characteristics of the fault gouge, reconstituted samples were prepared using a prefabricated sample mould with varying thickness, dip, water content, and clay content. The results showed that increasing the fault thickness, inclination, water content, and clay content significantly reduced the UCS from 46% to up to 63%. Among these, water and clay content were determined to be the most sensitive parameters affecting the geo-mechanical behaviours.

Further to assess the interplay between fault parameters and mine excavation, a finite-element-based numerical simulation was performed to assess the influence of the fault geometry, fault-crest distance, and dumping conditions on slope stability. The results showed that fault dip is the most significant parameter in controlling stress redistribution and deformation. Two dominant fault slip mechanisms were recognized: Type I is linked to slip due to a reduction in normal stress and loss of confinement, and Type II involves a reduction in normal stress and a significant increase in shear stress, leading to fault slip failure. Among these slip failures, Type II is the most common mechanism that regulates slope instability.

To validate excavation-induced fault reactivation mechanisms, combined physical and numerical Modelling studies were ultimately conducted using scaled instrumented models. Progressive excavation towards the fault plane produced increasing crack propagation, deformation, and stress concentration patterns consistent with numerical simulation results. Slope collapse consistently occurred when the excavation approached within 20 cm (equivalent to 20m in the field) of the fault plane under prototype conditions. Additional analyses on fault geometry demonstrated that increasing fault dip and thickness significantly reduce slope stability and accelerate shear-controlled failure mechanisms. The study provides a detailed understanding of fault-controlled instability and aids in the design of safer slopes, excavation planning, and hazard assessment in faulted opencast coal mines. &nbsp

Keywords: Slope stability, Opencast mine, Fault gouge, Fault reactivation, Numerical and Physical modelling
